name: Benzatropine
lead: Benzatropine (benztropine in the United States and Japan, sold under the brand name Cogentin) is an anticholinergic and antihistamine prescription medicine used to ease tremor, stiffness and muscle spasms in Parkinson's disease and to treat movement side effects of antipsychotic drugs.[1][2] Its appearance relevance comes through those effects: by calming visible tremor, involuntary facial or neck muscle contractions and, in some cases, drooling and salivary gland swelling caused by other medicines, it can restore steadier movement and a more natural facial expression.[1][3]

Medications that treat schizophrenia can cause involuntary muscle effects, such as spasms of the face, neck and jaw, restlessness and tremor. Because these are visible in posture, expression and gait, a drug that relieves them changes how a person looks and moves in everyday life. Benzatropine is one of the longest-established drugs for this purpose, and it is also used off-label for drooling [1][3].

It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, restoring balance with dopamine signalling, and may also affect dopamine reuptake.[1] Wikipedia describes it as selectively antagonising M1 and M3 receptors, with animal studies placing its anticholinergic activity at about half that of atropine.[2] It was approved for medical use in the United States in 1954 and has been in clinical use for more than 50 years.[1][2]

Published evidence includes reviews of dystonia and Parkinson's treatment and a case report with systematic review on clozapine-induced parotid swelling.[4][5][3] Benzatropine has no cosmetic indication. Benzatropine is not a looksmaxxing compound, and no community material about it as an appearance aid was found; it is documented here for the visible movement and facial effects it addresses.

chain: Calms drug-induced tremor, dystonia and drooling
Steadier, more natural facial and body movement
angle.text: Benzatropine is used to relieve visible side effects of antipsychotics such as facial muscle spasms, tremor and hypersalivation. Its appearance benefit is restoring ordinary movement and expression where these effects are present.

infobox: Benefit begins within about two hours and lasts up to about ten hours[2]

paras: Benzatropine has no direct cosmetic role. In a published case, benzatropine combined with terazosin resolved painful parotid swelling and hypersalivation caused by clozapine, a visible facial change.[3] More broadly, it relieves the muscle spasms and tremor that other drugs can cause, which can alter facial expression, head position and gait.

A 2014 BMJ Clinical Evidence systematic review of dystonia, a condition of involuntary muscle contractions, lists benzatropine among the interventions it evaluated, alongside amantadine, baclofen and botulinum toxins [4].

It is used for Parkinson's disease, drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia, parkinsonism and akathisia, and sometimes off-label for dystonia and drooling.[1][2][4][5] Wikipedia describes it as a second-line treatment for Parkinson's disease that improves tremor and may ease rigidity and bradykinesia; it is reported as not useful for tardive dyskinesia.[2] Off-label uses described by Grokipedia include chronic sialorrhea and intractable hiccups.[1]

Wikipedia notes that benzatropine reduces extrapyramidal side effects of antipsychotics, including akathisia, is a second-line Parkinson's treatment, is sometimes used for dystonia, and is not useful for tardive dyskinesia [2]. A 2005 review of alternatives to levodopa in early Parkinson's disease places such drugs in the context of dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors, which are used in younger patients [5].

It antagonizes muscarinic receptors and crosses the blood-brain barrier; it is structurally related to atropine and has antihistamine activity.[1] Wikipedia describes selective antagonism of M1 and M3 receptors, antihistamine activity close to that of mepyramine, and an atypical dopamine reuptake inhibition that may help akathisia.[2] Wikipedia also lists it as a functional inhibitor of acid sphingomyelinase [2]. In animal studies its anticholinergic activity was about half that of atropine [2].

Grokipedia reports limited oral bioavailability from poor gastric absorption and extensive first-pass liver metabolism, and ready entry to the brain.[1] Wikipedia gives metabolism in the liver, kidney excretion, an elimination half-life of 12 to 24 hours and a duration of action of about 10 hours.[2] Benefit is reported to begin within about two hours [2].

Reported effects are mostly anticholinergic: dry mouth, blurred vision, cognitive changes, drowsiness, constipation, urinary retention, fast heart rate and reduced appetite, and Wikipedia notes severe delirium and hallucinations mainly in overdose.[2] Grokipedia adds anhidrosis, hyperthermia and cognitive impairment and advises caution in hot environments and in people with glaucoma or prostatic enlargement.[1] Wikipedia notes that studies disagree on whether anticholinergics raise tardive dyskinesia risk, and that anticholinergics may impair long-term memory formation.[2] Anticholinergic burden in people with schizophrenia has itself been the subject of a registered study.[6]
Benzatropine has the formula C21H25NO and a molar mass of about 307.4 g per mole, and is formulated as the methanesulfonate (mesylate) salt.[2]

Benzatropine was approved for medical use in the United States in 1954 [2]. The name benzatropine was introduced under the WHO international nonproprietary naming scheme in 1959, while the United States uses the name benztropine [2]. Wikipedia also records its veterinary use for priapism in stallions [2].

The name benzatropine is the international nonproprietary and British approved name, introduced under the WHO scheme in 1959, whereas benztropine is used in the United States and Japan; Australia adopted the international form in 2015. Cogentin is a leading brand. Wikipedia reports more than 2 million US prescriptions in 2020. It is prescription-only in the United States and Australia.[2]

Wikipedia reports that benzatropine was identified in a high-throughput screen as an agent that promotes oligodendrocyte differentiation, and that in preclinical multiple sclerosis models it reduced clinical symptoms and enhanced remyelination (Nature, 2013).[2] Analogues have been studied in rats as antagonists of methamphetamine self-administration.[2]

A 2014 BMJ Clinical Evidence systematic review of dystonia treatment found 19 studies meeting its inclusion criteria and presented effectiveness and safety information for interventions including acupuncture, amantadine, baclofen, benzatropine, biofeedback and botulinum toxins [4]. A 2005 review addressed alternatives to levodopa in the initial treatment of early Parkinson's disease [5].

A 2012 case report and systematic review described a 58-year-old man whose painful bilateral parotid swelling and hypersalivation on clozapine, which had responded only partly to dose changes and antihypersalivatory drugs, resolved with benzatropine plus terazosin. The swelling returned when the doses were missed and resolved again once he resumed them. The authors found that none of the published articles set out a treatment regimen for clozapine-induced parotid swelling [3].

A 2024 pharmacovigilance study of the WHO safety database (VigiBase) analysed 421 paediatric reports of drug-related catatonia and found a disproportionality signal for benzatropine in adolescents (reporting odds ratio 193; 95 percent CI 104.1-361.6) [8]. A registered phase 2 trial that began in 2001 tested benztropine for cocaine craving [7], and a registered study of anticholinergic burden in schizophrenia was terminated with two participants [6]. Studies of benzatropine for appearance outcomes have not been published.

card.summary: An anticholinergic prescription drug that relieves tremor, muscle spasms and drug-induced drooling, restoring steadier movement and expression.
card.note: Prescription-only; anticholinergic effects include heat intolerance, confusion and urinary retention.

quick.overview:
Benzatropine is an older anticholinergic prescription drug. Doctors use it to reduce tremor and rigidity in Parkinson's disease and to treat muscle spasms, restlessness and stiffness caused by antipsychotics.

Appearance-related uses are indirect: calmer facial and neck muscles, less tremor, and in some reports less drooling or salivary gland swelling.
quick.mechanism: It competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system, offsetting the excess cholinergic activity that follows dopamine blockade, and has antihistamine properties as well [1].
quick.risks: Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, reduced sweating with overheating risk, and memory or confusion problems; long-term anticholinergic use has been linked to cognitive risks. It is prescription-only.
